entries.title: AUSTRIAN SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS
entries.body: A school of economic thought that theorizes the market as a set of voluntary individual interactions, emphasizes the spontaneity of economic order, and criticizes state interventions. The Austrian School defends the role of private property, freedom of contract, and free trade, while criticizing the disruptive effects of money creation on the economy. Its contributors, such as Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises or Friedrich Hayek, worked on concepts such as price formation, the function of money, the dynamics of capital, or the subjective theory of value. The Austrian School criticizes socialism for its inability to carry out efficient economic calculation, and favors a liberal approach. It values the free market and sees state interventionism as a source of economic imbalances. Many bitcoiners adhere to these ideas and consider that Bitcoin is a tool in harmony with this philosophy because of its distributed nature, the limitation of its money creation, and its ability to operate independently of state intervention.

entries.title: BLOCK EXPLORER
entries.body: Online or local tool that transforms the raw data of the Bitcoin blockchain into a structured, easily human-readable format. The explorer generally includes a search engine to easily locate a specific block, transaction or address.

entries.title: BLOCK HEADER
entries.body:
The block header is a data structure serving as the main component in the construction of a Bitcoin block. Each block is composed of a header and a list of transactions. The block header contains the crucial information that ensures the integrity and validity of a block within the blockchain. The block header contains 80 bytes of metadata and consists of the following elements:
* The block version;
* The hash of the previous block;
* The Merkle root of the transactions;
* The block timestamp;
* The difficulty target;
* The nonce.

For example, here is the header of block no. 785,530 in hexadecimal format, mined by Foundry USA on April 15, 2023:

```text
00e0ff3f5ffe3b0d9247dc437e18edc19252e4517cee941752d501000000000000000000206bde3a10826e2acb2f28fba70463601c789293d0c9c4348d7a0d06711e97c0bcb13a64b2e0051743f09a40
```

If we break down this header, we can recognize:
* The version: 

```text
00e0ff3f
```

* The previous hash:

```text
5ffe3b0d9247dc437e18edc19252e4517cee941752d501000000000000000000
```

* The Merkle root:

```text
206bde3a10826e2acb2f28fba70463601c789293d0c9c4348d7a0d06711e97c0
```

* The timestamp:

```text
bcb13a64
```

* The target:

```text
b2e00517
```

* The nonce: 

```text
43f09a40
```

To be valid, a block must have a header that, once hashed with `SHA256d`, produces a hash less than or equal to the difficulty target.

entries.title: CANTILLON EFFECT
entries.body:
An economic phenomenon described by the Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon in the 18th century, according to which the injection of new money into an economy does not spread uniformly. The first recipients of this newly created money (banks, financial institutions, states) can use it before prices rise, while the last to receive it (wage earners, savers, populations furthest from the banking system) suffer the price increase without having benefited from early access to this liquidity. This creates a hidden redistribution of wealth in favor of those who are close to the source of monetary issuance.

Bitcoin is sometimes presented as a response to this effect: its monetary issuance is programmed, predictable and governed by the protocol. The block subsidy, which decreases over the course of the halvings, is distributed to miners in return for work, without any central authority being able to decide to arbitrarily create new units. There is therefore no privileged intermediary able to capture the value of money creation before the rest of the network.

entries.title: E-GOLD
entries.body:
A digital currency system backed by gold, founded in 1996 by Douglas Jackson and Barry Downey. Users could open accounts denominated in grams of precious metals (gold, silver, platinum, palladium) stored in vaults. Transfers between accounts were instant and irrevocable.

At its peak in 2006, e-gold processed more than 2 billion dollars of transactions per year and had about 3.5 million accounts. The system attracted both legitimate users and illicit activity, due to the absence of identity verification.

In 2007, the US government indicted the operators of e-gold for operating an unlicensed money transmitting business and for money laundering. The company pleaded guilty in 2008. The shutdown of e-gold illustrated the vulnerability of centralized digital currency systems to state action, an observation that influenced the decentralized design of Bitcoin.

entries.title: ECASH - DAVID CHAUM
entries.body: A protocol proposed by David Chaum in 1982, which is one of the first digital currency systems designed to preserve users' anonymity. It relies on public-key cryptography principles to create a digital currency that can be exchanged securely and anonymously. eCash works by creating digital tokens signed by a bank. It is therefore an evolution of deposit banks, without being decentralized. During transactions, these tokens are transferred between the parties without revealing the users' identity, thus preserving their privacy. eCash is considered a precursor of cryptocurrencies. It also frequently comes up in discussions around Bitcoin, some wanting to use eCash-like systems as an overlay. Today, the trend is rather toward so-called "federated Chaumian" systems such as Fedimint.

entries.title: ECASH - XEC
entries.body: A cryptocurrency system, previously known as Bitcoin Cash ABC (BCHA), resulting from a hard fork of Bitcoin Cash (BCH). The eCash fork occurred on November 15, 2020 at block 661,648, resulting from a conflict within the Bitcoin Cash community.

entries.title: ECDH
entries.body: A cryptographic key exchange method built on the principles of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, but which uses elliptic curves to provide a high level of security with smaller key sizes. This protocol allows two parties to generate a shared secret using their public and private key pairs, without ever having to exchange the private keys themselves. The shared secret can then be used to encrypt subsequent communication. This algorithm is sometimes found in Bitcoin improvement proposals, notably BIP-0047 or BIP-0352 for deriving fresh receiving addresses from a static identifier.

entries.title: ECDSA
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*". It is a digital signature algorithm built on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). It is a variant of the DSA (*Digital Signature Algorithm*) algorithm. ECDSA uses the properties of elliptic curves to provide security levels comparable to those of traditional public-key algorithms, such as RSA, while using significantly smaller keys. ECDSA allows the generation of key pairs (public key and private key) as well as the creation and verification of digital signatures.

In the context of Bitcoin, ECDSA is used to derive public keys from private keys. It is also used to sign transactions, in order to satisfy a script to unlock bitcoins and spend them. The elliptic curve used on Bitcoin within ECDSA is `secp256k1`, defined by the equation `y^2 = x^3 + 7`. This algorithm has been used since the early days of Bitcoin in 2009. Today, it shares its place with the Schnorr protocol, another digital signature algorithm introduced with Taproot in 2021.

entries.title: ECLAIR
entries.body:
A major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the Scala language. Eclair is developed by the French company ACINQ.

*Note that "Eclair" was also the name of a Lightning wallet for mobile devices, developed by the same company. Today, this wallet is no longer maintained.*

entries.title: ECLIPSE
entries.body: An attack that consists of isolating and controlling a node's communications in a network by creating an artificial environment around it. The goal is to filter or manipulate the information received and sent by this node, thus cutting it off from its legitimate peers. In the context of Bitcoin, this technique can be used to mislead a node, to censor or alter the data it receives or sends, or to carry out double-spend attacks.

entries.title: EDGE NODE
entries.body:
A specialized routing node serving as an intermediary between Taproot Assets wallets and the classic Lightning network. An *edge node* maintains public Bitcoin channels to the Lightning network and unannounced Taproot Assets channels with its clients. Its main function is to convert Taproot Assets into BTC (and vice versa) when routing payments, via standard HTLCs.

Concretely, a wallet holding a Taproot asset (for example a dollar stablecoin) can pay any BOLT-11/12 Lightning invoice: the *edge node* receives the asset from the client, performs the conversion and routes the payment in BTC over the network. Conversely, an incoming Lightning payment in BTC can be converted into a Taproot Asset before being delivered to the client. The *edge node* provides quotes (*quotes*) for each conversion and collects routing fees. It never takes custody of the client's funds: exchanges are atomic thanks to HTLCs.

entries.title: ELECTRS
entries.body: An *open-source* implementation of Electrum Server written in Rust. The role of an electrs is therefore to maintain a complete index of Bitcoin addresses and transactions from the blockchain provided by a full node, in order to easily and quickly make queries from wallet software (such as Electrum for example).

entries.title: ELECTRUM
entries.body: A Bitcoin wallet founded in November 2011 by Thomas Voegtlin, which allows users to manage their funds without downloading the entire blockchain thanks to an SPV (*Simplified Payment Verification*) system. Because it has existed since the very beginning of the 2010s and because of its involvement in the development of Bitcoin, Electrum holds a historic place as wallet software.

entries.title: ELECTRUM LIGHTNING
entries.body: An implementation of the Lightning Network written in Python specifically for the Electrum software.

entries.title: ELECTRUM SERVER
entries.body: An indexer implemented on a Bitcoin full node that allows Electrum wallet software (or any other wallet that supports them) to operate without downloading the entire Bitcoin blockchain. An Electrum Server maintains a complete index of Bitcoin addresses and transactions, which makes it possible to make fast queries from other software. To put it simply, an Electrum Server acts as a kind of bridge between wallet software and a Bitcoin node that has the blockchain.

entries.title: ELEMENTS
entries.body:
An open source blockchain platform for deploying federated sidechains pegged to Bitcoin or standalone blockchains. Launched in June 2015, Elements is built on the Bitcoin Core code and extends it with advanced features: *Confidential Transactions* (hidden amounts and asset types), *Issued Assets* (issuance of several types of assets on the same chain), additional opcodes and *Federated Peg* (two-way peg with Bitcoin via a federation of signers).

Consensus relies on blocks signed by a federation of participants with aligned interests, which eliminates the risk of multi-block reorganizations and speeds up transaction finality compared to proof-of-work mining. Liquid Network, the most widely used sidechain in the Bitcoin ecosystem, is the main production implementation of Elements.

entries.title: ELTOO
entries.body:
A general-purpose protocol for Bitcoin second layers that makes it possible to define how to jointly manage the ownership of a UTXO. Eltoo was designed by Christian Decker, Rusty Russell and Olaoluwa Osuntokun, notably to solve the problems associated with the mechanisms for negotiating the state of Lightning channels, that is, between opening and closing. The Eltoo architecture simplifies the negotiation process by introducing a linear state management system, replacing the penalty-based approach with a more flexible and less punitive update method. This protocol requires the use of a new type of SigHash that makes it possible to take no input into account in the signature of a transaction. This SigHash was first called `SIGHASH_NOINPUT`, then `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` (*Any Previous Output*). Its implementation is planned in BIP-0118.

*Eltoo is sometimes also called "LN-Symmetry".*

entries.title: ENDIANNESS
entries.body: Refers to the order in which a sequence of bytes is arranged and interpreted in computing. There are two types: "*big-endian*", where the most significant byte (the one with the highest weight) is stored first, and "*little-endian*", where the least significant byte (the one with the lowest weight) is stored first.

entries.title: ENGRAVING
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *engraving* refers to an optional data string that the holders of a contract can successively inscribe in the history of its transitions. Accessible notably via the RGB21 interface, this feature makes it possible to add commemorative or descriptive information without changing the validity of the operations. It enriches the contract's history by integrating additional metadata.

entries.title: ENTROPY
entries.body:
Entropy, in the context of cryptography and information, is a quantitative measure of the uncertainty or unpredictability associated with a data source or a random process. Entropy plays a crucial role in the security of cryptographic systems, notably in the generation of keys and random numbers. High entropy guarantees that the generated keys are sufficiently unpredictable and resistant to brute-force attacks, where an attacker tries all possible combinations to guess the key. 

In the context of Bitcoin, entropy is used to generate private keys or seeds. When creating a deterministic and hierarchical wallet, the mnemonic phrase is built from a random number, itself derived from an entropy source. The phrase is then used to generate several private keys, in a deterministic and hierarchical manner, in order to create spending conditions on UTXOs. 

It is essential to have a quality entropy source to guarantee the security of cryptographic systems. Entropy sources can be physical processes, such as electronic noise or thermal variations, or software processes, such as pseudo-random number generators.

entries.title: ENTROPY - CHAIN ANALYSIS
entries.body:
In the specific context of chain analysis, entropy is also the name of a metric, derived from Shannon entropy, invented by LaurentMT. This metric measures the analysts' lack of knowledge about the exact configuration of a Bitcoin transaction. In other words, the higher a transaction's entropy, the more difficult the task of identifying the movements of bitcoins between the inputs and the outputs becomes for analysts.

In practice, entropy reveals whether, from the point of view of an external observer, a transaction presents multiple possible interpretations, based solely on the amounts of the inputs and outputs, without taking into account other external or internal *patterns* and heuristics. A high entropy is therefore synonymous with better privacy for the transaction.

Entropy is defined as the binary logarithm of the number of possible combinations. Here is the formula used, with `E` the entropy of the transaction and `C` the number of possible interpretations:
```math
E = \log_2(C)
```
Taking into account the values of the UTXOs involved in the transaction, the number of interpretations `C` represents the number of ways in which the inputs can be associated with the outputs. In other words, it determines the number of interpretations that a transaction can give rise to from the point of view of an outside observer analyzing it.

entries.title: ENVOY
entries.body: Mobile application developed by Foundation Devices. Envoy serves both as a standalone Bitcoin wallet and as a companion interface for the Passport *hardware wallet*: it allows you to set up the device, update its firmware and sign transactions via QR codes exchanged with the Passport, which operates *air-gapped*.

entries.title: EPHEMERAL ANCHORS
entries.body:
Relay policy proposal that allows zero-fee transactions to be broadcast on the network, provided they are accompanied by a child transaction that pays sufficient fees for both. The parent transaction contains a zero-value output with an *anyone-can-spend* script, which allows any participant in the network to create a child transaction that spends this ephemeral output, attaching the appropriate fees to it at the time of broadcast.

This mechanism solves a fundamental problem of contract protocols such as the Lightning Network: transactions are signed by the participants well before they are broadcast, which makes it impossible to determine in advance a fee rate suited to network conditions. *Ephemeral anchors* make it possible to defer the choice of fees to the time of publication, offering a form of "fee sponsorship" (*fee sponsorship*) accessible to any party, whether or not they are a beneficiary of the transaction's other outputs.

This proposal builds on the v3 transaction relay rules and on *package relay*. It is an evolution of the traditional Lightning Network *anchor outputs*, themselves based on the *CPFP carve-out* rule. Bitcoin Core introduced the standardized *Pay-To-Anchor* (P2A) output type to implement this mechanism. *Ephemeral anchors* are also an effective countermeasure against transaction pinning attacks.

entries.title: EREBUS
entries.body: A very sophisticated form of attack against the Bitcoin network that allows a malicious Internet service provider to isolate specific Bitcoin nodes. It is therefore a form of Eclipse attack. The Erebus attack exploits the structure of the Internet, in particular the chokepoints (or "*bottlenecks*") in routing between autonomous systems (AS). An attacker, by controlling an autonomous system, can manipulate network traffic to isolate a Bitcoin node from the rest of the network, and thus make it believe in a false state of the blockchain (blocks or transactions not known by the node). This isolation can lead to double spends or censorship against the isolated node. This attack has been made much more difficult since version 0.20.0 of Bitcoin Core and the introduction of Asmap.

entries.title: ERLAY
entries.body:
Network protocol proposal whose objective is to improve the efficiency of relaying unconfirmed transactions between Bitcoin nodes.

Currently, each transaction is propagated through a system in which each node broadcasts the transaction it learns of to all of its peers. The problem is that this leads to a great deal of redundancy and bandwidth use for duplicates. Many transaction broadcasts turn out to be useless, because the recipient already knows about these transactions, and each node only needs to know each transaction once. Erlay proposes to limit by default to 8 the number of peers to which a node directly sends the transactions it learns of, and then to use a reconciliation process based on the *minisketch* library to share the missing transactions more efficiently.

Erlay would reduce bandwidth consumption by about 40%, which would make running a full node more accessible to users with limited Internet connections, and would therefore promote better decentralization of the network. This protocol would also maintain a nearly constant bandwidth consumption as the number of connections increases. This means it would be much simpler for node operators to accept a very large number of connections from their peers, which would strengthen the security of the Bitcoin network by reducing the risks of partitioning, whether intentional or accidental. In addition, Erlay would make it harder to determine the origin node of a transaction, which would thus increase privacy for users of nodes that do not operate over Tor.

Erlay is proposed in BIP-0330.

entries.title: ESCROW
entries.body:
Mechanism by which funds are entrusted to a trusted third party who holds them until the conditions agreed between the parties are met. In French, it is called a "séquestre". Escrow is commonly used in commercial transactions to protect both the buyer and the seller.

In the context of Bitcoin, escrow can be implemented in different ways. The most common method uses multisig addresses (2-of-3), where three keys are distributed among the buyer, the seller and an arbitrator. The funds can only be released if at least two of the three parties sign the transaction, which allows dispute resolution without any single party controlling the funds.

Timelocks can also be built in to ensure that the funds do not remain locked indefinitely. On-chain escrow is notably used by peer-to-peer exchange platforms such as Bisq or HodlHodl to secure transactions without a centralized third party.

entries.title: ESMPPS
entries.body: Acronym for "*Equalized Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. ESMPPS aims to distribute the reward fairly among all submitted shares, regardless of when they were submitted or the pool's luck. It works essentially like SMPPS, but with an added notion of equality for the submitted shares.

entries.title: ESPLORA
entries.body: *Open source* block explorer developed by Blockstream and publicly accessible at `blockstream.info`. The interface takes the form of a single-page web application (*SPA*) that consumes the HTTP API provided by *esplora-electrs*, a modified version of *Electrs* in Rust that indexes the blockchain from a Bitcoin Core node. The tool also supports Liquid and Elements-based chains, with handling of confidential transactions and *peg-in/peg-out* operations.

entries.title: ETF
entries.body:
An ETF (*Exchange-Traded Fund*) is an exchange-listed investment fund that replicates the performance of an asset or a basket of assets. Unlike a traditional fund, an ETF is bought and sold continuously on stock markets, like an ordinary share.

In the context of Bitcoin, spot Bitcoin ETFs, approved in the United States in January 2024, allow institutional and individual investors to gain exposure to the price of bitcoin without directly holding the asset. The fund buys and holds actual bitcoins on behalf of its unit holders. There are also futures ETFs (*futures*) that are based on derivative contracts rather than physical holding.

Bitcoin ETFs involve a trusted intermediary (the fund manager) and fees, and do not confer the individual sovereignty provided by direct holding in self-custody.

entries.title: EXIT TRANSACTION
entries.body:
Pre-signed Bitcoin transaction allowing a user to unilaterally withdraw their funds from Spark (or a statechain) to the main layer, without requiring the cooperation of the *Spark Entity*.

The exit transaction is created and co-signed by the user and the SE at the time the user receives funds on Spark. Each new owner obtains an exit transaction with a shorter relative *timelock* than that of the previous owner. This decreasing hierarchy of timelocks ensures that the current owner can always publish their transaction on-chain before the previous owners, thus preventing double-spend attempts. To exit, the user broadcasts the exit transaction along with its parent transactions on the Bitcoin network.

entries.title: EXTENSION BLOCK
entries.body:
Proposal that aims to increase Bitcoin's transaction capacity by adding a secondary block attached to the main block via a commitment in the coinbase transaction. This concept was initially proposed by Johnson Lau in 2013 under the name "*auxiliary blocks*", then taken up in March 2017 by Christopher Jeffrey, Joseph Poon, Fedor Indutny and Stephen Pair, in the midst of the Blocksize War. In this mechanism, a miner includes in the coinbase an output `OP_RETURN` that contains the Merkle root of an extension block. This secondary block has its own UTXO set and its own consensus rules, while still being validated by the full nodes that support it. Funds move between the main chain and the extension block through "resolution transactions" that consolidate the inputs and outputs between the two sets.

This proposal was never formalized as a BIP and was not activated. It was criticized for its complexity, for its effects similar to those of a hard fork from an economic point of view, and for the absence of real benefits compared to SegWit.

entries.title: EXTRA TRANSACTION PROOF
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, the ETP is the part of the Anchor that incorporates the additional data essential for validating a Tapret-type commitment (in the context of Taproot). It includes, among other things, the internal public key associated with the Taproot script and the specific information required for the *Script Path Spend*. This component thus ensures the precise verification of the cryptographic commitments.

entries.title: EXTRA-NONCE
entries.body:
Field used in the `scriptSig` of a block's coinbase transaction, which allows a greater number of possibilities to be tested to obtain a hash lower than or equal to the difficulty target, in addition to the classic nonce which is located directly in the header of each block.

Modifying the extra-nonce in the coinbase transaction changes the identifier of this transaction, and therefore the Merkle root of all the transactions in the block, which also modifies the block header. This allows the miner to keep searching for hashes when the range of the classic nonce is already exhausted, without changing the structure of their candidate block.

In the context of mining pools, the extra-nonce is often divided into two parts: one generated by the pool to identify each hasher, and another modified by the hasher in the search for a valid *share*. This allows the different hashers in the pool to work simultaneously on the same candidate block with the entire range of nonces, without duplicating the same work at the pool level.

entries.title: LABELING
entries.body:
Practice of assigning an annotation or a label to a specific UTXO in a Bitcoin wallet. For example, if I own a UTXO coming from a P2P purchase on Bisq with Charles, I could assign it the label "`Non-KYC Bisq Charles`".

Labeling is a good practice that helps to remember the origin or the intended destination of a UTXO, thus making it easier to manage funds and optimize privacy. Labeling is all the more important when it is used with *coin control*. Indeed, by allowing users to differentiate and precisely select UTXOs for their transactions, this practice helps avoid merging UTXOs from different sources. This limits the risks associated with the CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*) chain analysis heuristic, which can reveal the common ownership of a transaction's inputs.

entries.title: NATURAL BRANCHING / CHAINSPLIT
entries.body: A temporary split of the blockchain resulting from the near-simultaneous broadcast of several blocks by different miners at the same height. This situation occurs when two blocks, designated as `A` and `B`, are found almost simultaneously, causing a temporary division of the network. Since each node considers the first block it received as valid, but not everyone received the same block first, some of the nodes follow the chain containing block `A`, while the others follow the one with block `B`. This branching is resolved when one of the two competing chains overtakes the other in terms of accumulated work. At that moment, all the nodes of the network automatically agree on the longest chain (with the most accumulated work), a process called reorganization or resynchronization. These natural branchings are inherent to the distributed operation of Bitcoin. They are perfectly normal and resolve spontaneously after a few blocks (generally just one). If there are too many of them, these branchings can nevertheless be harmful, because they cause a waste of computing power on a branch that will eventually become obsolete.

entries.title: NETWORK EFFECT
entries.body:
An economic phenomenon in which the value or utility of a product or service increases as the number of its users grows. The more participants a network has, the more attractive it becomes to new users, creating a virtuous circle of adoption. This concept is closely related to Metcalfe's law.

The network effect is fundamental to understanding money: a currency has value only because other people accept it. The greater the number of people who accept a currency, the more useful that currency is as a medium of exchange. This mechanism explains the natural tendency toward a single monetary standard within an economy.

entries.title: NOSTR EVENT
entries.body:
Fundamental unit of data in the Nostr protocol. Any information transmitted on the Nostr network (text post, profile update, reaction, encrypted message, zap receipt...) takes the form of an event. An event is a JSON object containing seven fields:
* `id`: a unique identifier obtained by SHA-256 hashing of the serialized content,
* `pubkey`: the author's public key,
* `created_at`: the Unix timestamp,
* `kind`: the event type identified by an integer,
* `tags`: the structured metadata used to mention users, reference other events or add hashtags,
* `content`: the text content,
* `sig`: the Schnorr signature on secp256k1.

The `kind` field determines the nature of the event: kind 0 for profile metadata, kind 1 for text notes, kind 4 for encrypted direct messages, kind 7 for reactions or kind 9735 for zap receipts. Relays verify the signature before accepting an event, which guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the data.

entries.title: WALLET FINGERPRINT
entries.body:
A set of distinctive characteristics observable in the transactions made by a single Bitcoin wallet. These characteristics can include similarities in the use of script types, address reuse, the ordering of UTXOs, the position of change outputs, RBF (*Replace-by-Fee*) signaling, the version number, the `nSequence` field and the `nLockTime` field. 

Wallet fingerprints are used by analysts to trace the activities of a particular entity on the blockchain by identifying recurring patterns in its transactions. For example, a user who systematically sends their change to P2TR addresses (`bc1p…`) creates a characteristic fingerprint that can be used to track their future transactions. 

As LaurentMT explains in Space Kek #19 (a French-language podcast), the usefulness of wallet fingerprints in chain analysis increases significantly over time. Indeed, the growing number of script types and the increasingly gradual rollout of these new features by wallet software accentuate the differences. It is even sometimes possible to identify exactly the software used by the traced entity. It must therefore be understood that studying a wallet's fingerprint proves particularly relevant for recent transactions, more so than for those initiated in the early 2010s.
